The Linear Transformation
Look at the mapping from the bottom axis (x0) to the middle axis (x1). The linear layer multiplies each point by a weight of 2. Notice how the dashed lines spread outward, stretching the distances between the data points uniformly.

interactionPlan.concept: Deep neural networks transform data distributions sequentially, using linear layers to stretch or shift the data and non-linear layers like ReLU to fold or clip it.
learningObjectives: After engaging with this figure, the student will understand how stacked layers in a neural network sequentially reshape the input data distribution.
The student will be able to explain how the ReLU activation function introduces non-linearity by collapsing negative values to zero while preserving positive values.
interactionPlan.keyInsight: A neural network isn't just an algebraic equation; it is a sequence of geometric transformations that stretch, shift, and fold the data space layer by layer.

interactions.label: Linear Weight (w)
interactions.effect: Changes the spread of the data points mapped onto the x1 axis. Dashed lines stretch further out (high w) or cross over (negative w).
interactions.teaches: Linear weights scale and reflect the data distribution, determining how spread out the representations become.

interactions.label: Linear Bias (b)
interactions.effect: Shifts all mapped data points on the x1 axis uniformly to the left or right.
interactions.teaches: Biases translate the data distribution, which controls exactly which data points will fall into the negative region of the subsequent ReLU layer.

demo_steps.title: The Linear Transformation
demo_steps.narration: Look at the mapping from the bottom axis (x0) to the middle axis (x1). The linear layer multiplies each point by a weight of 2. Notice how the dashed lines spread outward, stretching the distances between the data points uniformly.
demo_steps.focus: The bottom set of dashed lines expanding outward from x0 to x1.

demo_steps.title: The ReLU Non-linearity
demo_steps.narration: Now look at the mapping from the middle axis (x1) to the top axis (x2). The ReLU function acts as a filter: positive points map straight up (identity), but negative points are snapped to exactly zero.
demo_steps.focus: The top set of dashed lines, specifically how the two leftmost points converge at x2 = 0.

demo_steps.title: Collapsing Data at Zero
demo_steps.narration: This collapsing of negative values is the crucial 'non-linearity' of neural networks. Without this 'folding' action, the network would only be able to perform basic stretching and shifting, no matter how many layers it had.
demo_steps.focus: The cluster of multiple data points occupying the exact same position at zero on the top axis.

demo_steps.title: Shifting the Activation Window
demo_steps.narration: Try adjusting the Linear Bias slider to -1. Notice how shifting the entire x1 distribution to the left forces more points into the negative region, causing them to hit the 'ReLU wall' and collapse to zero.
demo_steps.focus: The x1 axis shifting left and the increased number of points converging at x2 = 0.

interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Three horizontal axes (x0, x1, x2) stacked vertically and centrally aligned. Each axis has tick marks labeled from -1 to 1. Five data points originate on the x0 axis (solid circles at roughly -0.5, -0.25, 0, 0.25, 0.5). Dashed lines map these points to solid triangles on the x1 axis based on x1 = w * x0 + b. A second set of dashed lines maps the x1 points to solid triangles on the x2 axis based on x2 = max(0, x1). Place boxed text equations to the left of the mapping spaces (e.g., 'x1 = 2 * x0' and 'x2 = relu(x1)'), updating the x1 equation dynamically if the user changes the weight or bias.
